strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—natural-language-controllable editing of real-world driving videos—and presents a complete, end-to-end system (Applied/Systems contribution) that combines 3D scene decomposition, agentic orchestration, behavior simulation, and video diffusion refinement into a coherent pipeline.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a systems paper: quantitative comparison against two strong baselines (Cosmos, ChatSim) across five aspects, human user study (26 participants), ablations of both the behavior reviewer loop (Table 2) and the video diffusion tool (Table 3), a dedicated object grounding benchmark (Table 4), ablations of counterfactual behavior generation and unreasonable-instruction rejection (Tables 5-6), and per-module timing (Table 7).

The counterfactual behavior generation mechanism (building behavior combinations from original trajectories, filtering with map topology and compatibility constraints) and the iterative reviewer-agent feedback loop (adjusting CFG/on-road/no-collision guidance weights) are thoughtful design elements that measurably improve instruction alignment and traffic realism.

The supplementary material is exemplary in supporting reproducibility: full agent prompts (Figs. 12-16), explicit counterfactual mapping and compatibility tables (Tables 10-11), test scene IDs, and clearly documented failure cases (Figs. 10-11) and limitations (no pedestrian editing; VDM can alter inserted object appearance).

The reported results are substantial—roughly 2× appearance/behavior alignment over both baselines with much lower collision and off-road rates—supporting the central claim of jointly achieving controllability, photorealism, and traffic realism.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf components (GPT-4/GPT-4o, CogVideoX, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, 3DGS/OmniRe, SAM, Difix3D+ training recipe). The core novelty is primarily in system integration and heuristics rather than new algorithms; the counterfactual behavior vocabulary and compatibility logic are hand-designed (Tables 10-11), which limits generalization beyond the enumerated vehicle behaviors.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o (the same VLM used inside the pipeline) for appearance alignment, collision/off-road detection, and structure-related judgments, creating a potential circularity/favoritism concern; the behavior alignment metric also uses the authors' own heuristic behavior-description logic as ground truth. Independent or human-verified versions of these metrics would strengthen the claims.

The test set is small: 30 Waymo scenes, 8-second front-camera clips only, and scenes deliberately selected to have few pedestrians. Multi-object editing is claimed as a key capability but the main comparison instructions mostly target single objects; the harder multi-object tests appear only in trajectory-space ablations, not in the headline comparison.

Only two baselines are quantitatively compared, and both are argued to be weaker a priori (Cosmos lacks object-level control; ChatSim has known rendering weaknesses). Several closely related methods (SceneCrafter, DriveEditor, ChatDyn, SimSplat) are compared only via checkmarks in Table 8 rather than empirically, which weakens the 'significantly outperforms previous methods' claim.

Structure preservation and photorealism metrics structurally favor scene-graph-based pipelines over pixel-space editors like Cosmos; the paper acknowledges this qualitatively but does not disentangle it (e.g., evaluating Cosmos conditioned on preserved structure).

Editing time is long overall (~2 hrs reconstruction + 12 min refinement per edit) and the fine-tuned VDM stage requires ~4 days on 4×H100s, which limits practicality; the VDM also sometimes changes inserted vehicles' type/color (acknowledged), undermining the appearance-alignment guarantee for uncommon vehicles.
The system requires ground-truth object trajectories and a map as input (Section 3.1), which restricts applicability to well-annotated driving datasets and is not reflected in the framing.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: combining natural-language controllability, open-vocabulary object grounding, multi-object behavior editing, and traffic realism in one driving-scene editing pipeline, whereas prior methods (ChatSim, Cosmos, DriveEditor, SceneCrafter) each satisfy only a subset of these capabilities.

The system design is coherent and clearly explained: the scene-graph representation from 3DGS decomposition enables object-level editing, and the separation of agents (reasoning) from tools (fixed APIs) makes the pipeline interpretable and modular.

The counterfactual behavior combination mechanism is a thoughtful component: it preserves original behaviors while applying requested edits, and the supplementary material (Tables 10, 11, and Section 8.1) provides substantial detail on behavior token generation, compatibility pruning, and map-aware filtering, which supports reproducibility.

The evaluation covers five dimensions (photorealism, appearance/behavior alignment, structure preservation, traffic realism, user study) and includes ablations for the behavior feedback loop (Table 2), video refinement (Table 3), object grounding (Table 4), counterfactual generation (Tables 5-6), and per-module runtime (Table 7). The failure case analysis (median barriers, VDM altering vehicle type/color) is honest.

Quantitative and qualitative results show clear improvements over both baselines, particularly in behavior alignment (71.67% vs 32.86%) and traffic realism (collision rate 0.58% vs 3.16%), and the project page/code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a systems integration of existing components: 3DGS decomposition (OmniRe), trajectory simulation (LangTraj), video diffusion (CogVideoX, TrajectoryCrafter weights), text-to-3D (Hunyuan3D), and GPT-4/GPT-4o for all agents. The novelty lies in orchestration, prompt engineering, and heuristic behavior filtering rather than new algorithms or models, which limits scientific depth for a venue like ECCV. The paper would benefit from explicitly framing itself as an Applied/Systems contribution.

The evaluation set is small: 30 scenes from Waymo with 2-3 instructions per type, and the grounding ablation uses only 5 scenes / 50 queries. Several quantitative comparisons involve VLM-based judgments (GPT-4o is used both as a core system component and as the evaluator for appearance alignment and traffic realism), creating potential circularity and no validation of these proxy metrics against human judgment.

The system assumes ground-truth object trajectories and a scene map as input (Section 3.1), which substantially limits real-world applicability compared to purely video-based editors like Cosmos; this assumption is understated in the main claims.

Table 8 is a self-assessed capability table against prior work rather than a controlled experimental comparison, and no quantitative comparison is provided against other agent-based methods beyond ChatSim (e.g., AutoVFX, ChatDyn) or diffusion-based editors (DriveEditor, SceneCrafter), weakening the 'outperforms previous methods' claims. The Cosmos comparison also conflates representation-level advantages (scene-graph methods naturally preserve background structure) with method quality.

Some improvements are modest and the behavior refinement ablation shows residual failure rates remain high (70% alignment, 22.86% collision, 14.29% off-road even after refinement), which is not reconciled with the low violation rates reported in Table 1; the discrepancy in evaluation protocols between Table 1 and Table 2 deserves clarification.
Heavy dependence on proprietary models (GPT-4, GPT-4o) makes long-term reproducibility uncertain, and the user study with 26 participants is small relative to the strength of the user-study claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—natural-language-controlled editing of real-world driving videos for synthetic scenario generation—and delivers a complete, working system that demonstrably outperforms prior art (ChatSim, Cosmos) across photorealism, instruction alignment, structure preservation, and traffic realism, with large margins (e.g., 82.19% vs ~46% appearance alignment; 0.58% vs 3.16% collision rate).

The system design is well-motivated and clearly articulated: explicit 3DGS-based scene graph decomposition provides controllability, while specialized agents (Object Grounding, Behavior Editing with counterfactual behavior generation, Behavior Reviewer with an iterative feedback loop) plus a diffusion-based video refinement tool address known weaknesses of both agent-based pipelines (ChatSim) and implicit world models (Cosmos).

The counterfactual behavior generation (token-level expansion, compatibility pruning, map-aware filtering) and the reviewer-driven guidance adjustment loop (CFG weight increases, on-road/collision guidance, saving successful trajectories as guidance) are concrete, well-specified technical contributions, and their value is validated by ablations (Tables 2, 5, 6), including a novel evaluation of unreasonable-instruction rejection (93.33% vs 0%).

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a systems paper: five evaluation axes, a 26-participant user study, per-component ablations, per-module runtime comparison, open-vocabulary grounding benchmark against Grounding SAM and 4DLangSplat, and a detailed capability comparison table against prior methods.

Reproducibility is strong: all agent prompts are disclosed in full, test scene IDs are listed, training details (iterations, batch size, hardware) are given, and failure cases are honestly reported (median-barrier violations, VDM altering vehicle type/color). The limitations section is meaningful rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily Applied/Systems: the core components (OmniRe-style 3DGS decomposition, Hunyuan3D text-to-3D, LangTraj trajectory simulation, CogVideoX finetuning, GPT-4/4o agents) are largely existing; novelty lies in their orchestration, the counterfactual behavior engine, and the video refinement finetuning. This is acceptable for this contribution type, but reviewers should note the limited algorithmic novelty relative to the framing.

Evaluation methodology has a circularity risk: the behavior alignment metric and the traffic realism checks rely on the authors' own behavior description heuristics and GPT-4o as judge, while GPT-4o is also embedded inside the pipeline (grounding, reviewing). This shared machinery could bias results in the method's favor, particularly for the reported ~2x instruction-alignment gain.

The evaluation scale is modest: 30 Waymo scenes, ~2-3 instructions per type (roughly 240-300 test edits), only the front camera, vehicles only (pedestrians explicitly out of scope), and a single dataset. The user study involves only 26 participants. Broader validation would strengthen the claims of generality.
The system assumes ground-truth object trajectories and HD maps as input, which limits applicability to logs without such annotations and weakens the 'edit any real-world driving video' framing.

The video diffusion refinement is a double-edged sword: it improves FID/FVD but can alter the type/color of inserted vehicles (documented failure case), which directly conflicts with the instruction-alignment objective and is not quantified; an ablation measuring alignment degradation from VDM refinement is missing.

Baselines are limited to two methods (ChatSim, Cosmos); the concurrent scene-graph agent-based work SimSplat [28] is discussed but not empirically compared, and no comparison against diffusion-based editors like SceneCrafter/DriveEditor is provided, even in a limited form.

Cost and accessibility are significant: ~2 hours scene reconstruction per scene, 12 minutes video refinement per edit, and a 4xH100 finetune of ~4 days; the paper reports times but does not deeply discuss the practicality trade-off for the target use case.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—natural-language-controllable editing of real driving videos—and presents a well-designed, coherent framework (LangDriveCTRL) that combines explicit 3D scene graph decomposition with a feedback-driven agentic pipeline, clearly differentiating itself from both world models (Cosmos) and prior unimodal agentic pipelines (ChatSim, AutoVFX, ChatDyn).

The feedback-driven refinement loop is a genuine and well-argued contribution: the Behavior Reviewer and Video Reviewer agents iteratively validate intermediate results (trajectories and renderings) and adjust CFG/guidance weights and diffusion strength, directly addressing the error-accumulation problem of prior feed-forward pipelines. Figures 3, 6, and 10 provide convincing qualitative illustrations.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough for a systems paper: quantitative comparison against two strong SoTA baselines plus a constructed image-editing+I2V baseline, a user study, per-module ablations for every major component (object grounding, counterfactual behavior generation, behavior refinement, video refinement), a hallucination analysis (3D consistency, NTL-IoU), a 'coarse vs. ChatSim' ablation isolating the agentic architecture's contribution, unreasonable-instruction rejection testing, and a downstream 3D detection task demonstrating utility of the edited data.

The counterfactual behavior generation component is technically well-developed and formalized (token expansion, Cartesian product of candidates, compatibility-matrix pruning, map-aware filtering), with detailed rules in Tables 14–15 and a dedicated ablation showing 93% rejection of infeasible instructions.

Reproducibility support is strong: full agent prompts, heuristics for behavior description/validation, fine-tuning configuration, test scene IDs, and discussion of failure cases (e.g., median barrier crossing). The limitation that ground-truth trajectories and map are assumed is stated explicitly.

The paper is honest about the video diffusion tool's trade-off (photorealism vs. appearance preservation) and quantifies it rather than hiding it (Table 4), and reports mild hallucination degradation from refinement (Table 5).
weaknesses: Evaluation has potential circularity: appearance alignment uses GPT-4o (the same VLM family powering the agents) to judge edits, and the behavior alignment metric shares its underlying logic with the Behavior Reviewer's validation functions. Although the authors apply a uniform tracking-based protocol to all methods and use explicit trajectories only during editing, VLM-based judging of VLM-driven results raises self-preference and bias concerns that are not analyzed. Collision/off-road rates are also detected by VLM from sampled frames, which is noisy for a safety-relevant metric.

The test set is small and constrained: 30 Waymo scenes, 8-second videos, front camera only, scenes deliberately selected to have few pedestrians. The method is described as 'multi-modal' and general, but evidence is limited to vehicle editing on a single dataset; generalization of the fine-tuned CogVideoX tool beyond Waymo-style data is unclear.

Strong input assumptions reduce applicability: the pipeline requires provided ground-truth object trajectories and scene maps, and a ~2-hour per-scene 3D reconstruction preprocessing step. The efficiency comparison (17.1 min/edit) omits this preprocessing, which may matter for the claimed practicality in synthetic data generation.

Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf components (GPT-4/GPT-4o, 3DGS, SAM, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, CogVideoX): the contribution is primarily orchestration and feedback design rather than a new algorithmic core. This is acceptable for an applied/systems contribution, but the marginal novelty of individual agents (largely prompt-engineered heuristics, e.g., fixed weight update rules in the reviewer prompts) is modest.

Some quantitative claims are under-specified: how FID/FVD are computed over the small 30-scene set (frame counts, real-reference distribution), variance/confidence over the user study with 26 participants, and statistical significance of the gaps (e.g., structure distance 34.62 vs. 74.07) are not reported.

Comparison baselines, while reasonable, are limited: DriveEditor, SceneCrafter, and the concurrent SimSplat are discussed (Table 12) but not empirically compared, with the latter relegated to a feature-level qualitative statement.

Failure analysis is thin: only one common failure mode (median barrier) is presented; behavior description generation relies on hand-tuned thresholds (e.g., ±10° heading tolerance, 0.5m static threshold) whose robustness across dataset shifts is unexamined.

strengths: Well-motivated applied/systems contribution: the paper clearly identifies real limitations of both agentic pipelines (ChatSim) and world models (Cosmos) for natural-language driving scene editing, and the proposed combination of explicit 3D scene graphs with feedback-driven refinement addresses a genuine gap (controllability + photorealism + traffic realism simultaneously).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for an agentic system paper: quantitative comparison against two open-source SoTA baselines, an additional image-editing + image-to-video baseline, ablations for the behavior reviewer (Table 3), video reviewer (Table 4), counterfactual behavior generation (Tables 7-8), object grounding (Table 6), a coarse-vs-ChatSim comparison that isolates the architectural contribution from the diffusion refinement (Table 9), a hallucination analysis (Table 5), a downstream detection task (Table 11), and an honest failure-case section.

The feedback-loop design is concretely demonstrated (Figures 3, 6, 10) with measurable gains (e.g., overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%), showing the closed-loop refinement is not merely decorative.

Considerable engineering transparency: prompts for all agents, behavior token mappings, compatibility matrices, scene IDs, and per-module timing are provided, which supports reproducibility of the pipeline structure.

The paper is candid about assumptions (provided trajectories and maps), limited pedestrian handling, residual traffic violations in failure cases, and mild hallucinations introduced by video diffusion.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: nearly every component is an existing tool — OmniRe-style 3DGS decomposition, LangTraj trajectory simulation, Hunyuan3D insertion, CogVideoX (initialized from TrajectoryCrafter) for video refinement, SAM/GPT-4o for grounding. The reviewers are not learned or novel algorithms but hand-crafted heuristic rules (e.g., 'increase CFG weight by 1.0', 'multiply on-road guidance by 3.0', bisection of denoising strength) executed by a VLM/LLM. The 'multi-modal agents' framing overstates what is largely prompt engineering plus fixed update rules.

Evaluation scale and scope are small: only 30 Waymo scenes, 8-second 10 FPS front-camera videos, ~140 instructions, and scenes deliberately chosen to have few pedestrians. Generalization beyond Waymo-style data and beyond the covered instruction types is untested.

Potential circularity and bias in the metrics: appearance alignment and collision/off-road detection use GPT-4o — the same VLM powering the method's own agents — as judge; the behavior alignment metric reuses the system's own behavior-description/validation logic; the object-grounding ground truth uses SAM and a loose IoU>0.2 threshold on only 50 queries. These choices plausibly favor the proposed system, and no cross-model judge or human verification of the automated metrics is reported.

The method requires ground-truth object trajectories and an HD map as input (Section 3.1), which substantially reduces the practical applicability of 'natural-language-controllable editing of real-world videos'; this assumption deserves more prominence and ablation.

Baseline coverage is narrow: empirical comparison is limited to ChatSim (2024) and Cosmos, plus a constructed naive baseline; ChatDyn, AutoVFX, and the concurrent SimSplat are only discussed qualitatively in Table 12 despite being closely related agent-based methods.

Fairness of comparison is questionable: the video diffusion tool is heavily fine-tuned on Waymo-style data (40k+20k iterations on 4xH100) with a cycle-reconstruction strategy, while baselines use off-the-shelf settings; the downstream-task gain (Table 11) is small and the detection training setup appears weak (AP values near 0.01), making that experiment unconvincing.

Writing quality is uneven (e.g., 'it lack', inconsistent w.r.t. supplementary/main numbering, 'vs.' used as a figure caption label), and the user study (26 participants, forced choice among three methods) is too small to carry much weight.

Reproducibility of the full system depends on closed-source GPT-4/GPT-4o, a fine-tuned diffusion checkpoint on proprietary Waymo data, and numerous heuristics; no code or checkpoint release is stated.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-integrated system: the paper combines explicit 3D scene-graph decomposition, a multi-modal agentic pipeline, and diffusion-based refinement into a coherent framework for language-controllable driving scene editing, supporting removal, insertion, replacement, and multi-object behavior editing.

Strong and broad empirical evidence for an Applied/Systems contribution: quantitative comparisons against both an agentic baseline (ChatSim) and a world-model baseline (Cosmos) across photorealism, instruction alignment, structure preservation, traffic realism, and user study, plus timing/efficiency analysis (Table 1-2).

Well-designed ablations that isolate contributions: grounding agent vs. Grounding-SAM/4DLangSplat (Table 6), behavior and video reviewer feedback loops (Tables 3-4), counterfactual behavior generation including rejection of unreasonable instructions (Tables 7-8), and 'Ours (Coarse)' vs. ChatSim (Table 9) showing the agentic architecture itself is a substantial contribution beyond diffusion refinement.

Additional evidence strengthens the case: an extra ChronoEdit+Wan 2.2 baseline (Table 10), a downstream BEVFormer training-data study (Table 11), hallucination analysis of the video diffusion step (Table 5), and an honest failure-case discussion (median-barrier crossing).

Good reproducibility support: detailed implementation settings, per-module timings, test scene IDs, and full prompts/workflows for every agent in the supplementary material, with appropriate attribution to the many underlying components (3DGS, LangTraj, CogVideoX, Hunyuan3D, SAM, etc.).
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily system integration of existing components rather than novel algorithms; the technical novelty resides in agent design, counterfactual behavior generation, and feedback heuristics. This is acceptable for an Applied/Systems paper, but the paper occasionally frames the gains as if they come from fundamental advances rather than engineering.

Evaluation scale is limited: only 30 Waymo scenes, front camera only, 8-second clips, and scenes deliberately selected to have few pedestrians. Generalization to other datasets, viewpoints, and pedestrian-heavy scenes is untested.

Potential metric circularity: the behavior alignment metric and the behavior reviewer agent share the same behavior-description/validation logic (Section 8.1), which may favor outputs expressed in the system's own behavior token vocabulary. Similarly, appearance alignment and collision/off-road rates are judged by a VLM, introducing possible bias; human evaluation (26 participants) partially mitigates this but is small.

Behavior reviewer success saturates at ~51% overall success (Table 3), and a substantial fraction of cases still require diffusion-side correction; the paper could analyze remaining failure modes more systematically than the single failure case shown.
Heavy reliance on proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4o for the orchestrator and reviewers weakens reproducibility and adds cost; no ablation on the choice of LLM/VLM backbone is provided.

Practicality concerns: per-scene 3D reconstruction takes ~2 hours, and per-edit time (~17 min) limits interactive use; the fine-tuned CogVideoX training setup (4xH100, 48h per stage) is nontrivial to reproduce.

No quantitative comparison with the closely related concurrent work SimSplat (acknowledged only qualitatively in Section 7), and no comparison with other diffusion-based editors (DriveEditor, SceneCrafter) despite their inclusion in the capability table.
